---
title: "Paper"
subtitle: "The manuscript editor — clean, fast writing where citations and figures take care of themselves"
---

Paper is where you write. Your document is plain text with light formatting — headings,
**bold**, math like `$E = mc^2$`, tables — and Flux renders the pretty version live, in place.
The file on disk stays an ordinary Quarto `.qmd` the whole time: formatting marks hide
themselves except on the line you're editing, so the screen reads like a manuscript while the
text stays honest.

# The writing surface

- **The title pill** above the text shows the title and authors; click it to edit them (they're
  stored as the document's front matter). The small dot on the pill is the autosave
  indicator — you never save by hand.
- **Alt+O** toggles the left rail: the **Outline** (click a heading to jump) and the
  **Documents** picker — a project can hold several manuscripts (the main one wears a *main*
  badge, **+ New document** adds more), plus the *Context* group where your
  [agent's mission, notebook, and rules](../agents/collaboration.qmd) open as ordinary
  documents.
- Type **/** at the start of a line for the block palette: `/figure`, `/table`, `/equation`,
  `/citation`, `/heading`, `/callout`, and friends.
- **Ctrl+K** opens the command palette — everything in this guide is also in there by name.
- **Ctrl+Shift+E** shows the full-width reading preview (**Escape** returns); the ⌘K palette
  also switches between continuous and paginated views. Fold a section with **Ctrl+Shift+[**
  (unfold: **Ctrl+Shift+]**). Spellcheck is on by default, and the word count in the status
  bar opens a full statistics pane.

# Local corrections

Paper quietly fixes only unmistakable typing slips as soon as you finish the word: transposed
letters such as *compelx* and an accidental space such as *o bject*. Insertions, deletions, and
ambiguous spelling neighbors wait for sentence context instead of guessing. The replacement fades
into place and a small blue dot pulses beneath it; the caret never moves. This first correction
layer uses Harper in a dedicated local worker and sends no manuscript text anywhere.

Click a recently corrected word to see what changed. **Undo** restores the original and teaches
this project not to repeat that correction; **Add to dictionary** also remembers the word as
project vocabulary. Normal **Ctrl+Z** targets the most recent correction batch, so independent
word-by-word changes remain independently undoable. Project titles, authors, references, figure
captions, and recurring technical terms help form the local vocabulary, while acronyms,
mixed-case scientific names, numbers, code, math, citations, links, and table source are left
alone.

For terms that matter, select one word — ordinary selection and Vim visual mode work the same —
and click **Word tools** (the small book in the floating toolbar), or press **Shift+Alt+W**. You
can recognize its spelling at either scope:

- **Project** applies only inside the current Flux project. **Shift+Alt+D** toggles the selected
  word directly.
- **Personal** follows you across Flux projects on this device. **Alt+D** toggles it.

The buttons and shortcuts are true toggles, so selecting the term again removes it just as
quickly. Explicit dictionary terms are protected from ordinary corrections and also become
high-confidence candidates for nearby mechanical mistakes: after adding *iGluSnFR4f*, for
example, *IgluSnrf4* can resolve to the canonical spelling. Flux remains conservative around
plausible scientific variants — a stored *SLAP2* does not turn *SLAP3* into *SLAP2*.

**Word tools** also creates aliases. Select *iGluSnFR4f*, enter *igf*, choose Project or
Personal, and add it. The next time `igf` is typed as its own word, the delimiter (space,
punctuation, or Return) instantly morphs it into *iGluSnFR4f* with the same blue pulse. One
**Ctrl+Z** restores `igf`; clicking the pulsed expansion offers **Remove alias**, and every
saved alias has its own × button in **Word tools**. Project aliases take priority over Personal
aliases when both use the same short form.

The blue **Local** item in the status bar shows when the checker is ready and toggles it on or
off. The same switch is in **Settings › Paper › Local corrections** and the command palette.
This conservative local layer does not rephrase, make stylistic edits, or guess at scientific
compound spelling; those are choices, not safe automatic corrections.

An optional second lane runs at completed-sentence boundaries. Harper first identifies exact
unresolved spans and supplies a small local word neighborhood. The context model may keep the
source, select one local proposal, or propose a better nearby spelling when Harper omitted it —
for example, *wayus* can become *ways* instead of Harper's *way us*. This is not sentence
rewriting: a proposal must be one plain word, preserve case, remain within the selected typing-edit
envelope, survive a separate scientific-term preservation check when applicable, and receive a
fresh contextual approval. Flux then independently verifies that word with Harper and rechecks the
current document, protected syntax, dictionaries, learned vetoes, and the hard time limit. If you
keep typing, a safe result maps behind the caret; editing its source span cancels it.

The underline shows the complete decision lifecycle without interrupting typing:

- An unresolved Harper span fades in **red** as soon as the word is complete.
- If sentence judgment corrects it, the line turns **blue**, the replacement morphs into place,
  and both fade away.
- If judgment leaves it alone, the line turns **orange** and remains. Click it to see Flux's
  structured reason and the relevant words it considered. This is a concise decision record, not
  hidden model reasoning.

Opening a document that already contains text gets the same red treatment without any editing:
Flux quietly scans the existing prose in the background and underlines what the local checker
flags, a few hundred marks at most. These are flags only — nothing is corrected, and the sentence
judge is not consulted for old text. Click a flag to see why it's marked; edit anywhere in that
sentence and the normal correction lanes take over from there. The scan skips the sentence you
are actively writing in, along with code, math, tables, and the other protected regions.

Settings offers three judgment envelopes. **Standard** is the default: one typing edit for short
words and two otherwise. **Aggressive** can explore three edits for words of nine or more letters.
**Really aggressive** explores every bounded candidate, allows three edits from seven letters and
four from ten, and is deliberately available for testing the high-recall edge. All three preserve
the same no-rewrite, syntax, scientific morphology, dictionary, contextual approval, local-lexicon,
and exact-source safety gates. Wider modes can be slower and still abstain when those gates fail.

**Flux managed** is the default contextual provider. In Settings, install the 2.33 GB Qwen3 4B
Instruct 2507 model explicitly; the download resumes after interruption, is SHA-256 verified under
`FluxConfig/Models/corrections/`, and can be unloaded or removed there. Flux owns a pinned
`llama-server` helper on authenticated loopback and never starts it on the Home screen. Apple
Silicon packages fully offload to Metal, Linux packages use the pinned Vulkan backend when a GPU is
available, and Settings names the active acceleration path. “Ready” means the model has produced a
schema-valid non-thinking answer, not merely that its process is listening. Builds that installed
the earlier hybrid Qwen3 artifact show **Update local model**; the verified update replaces it in
place with Instruct 2507.

An existing Ollama installation can be selected as an advanced local provider. Flux explicitly
warms the selected Ollama model, holds it for 15 minutes, and fixes its context at 2,048 tokens so a
small correction request cannot accidentally allocate the model's much larger default context.
Provider loading is allowed a longer background deadline, but a correction still has only the
editor's short silent-application window; a late result never changes the manuscript. GPT-5.6 Luna
is separately opt-in: its API key is OS-encrypted, requests use `store: false`, Settings discloses
the payload and shows the session cost estimate, and a local failure never activates cloud.

Personal guidance, project guidance, dialect, explicit terms, aliases, and learned “leave alone”
decisions all feed this bounded judgment. **Reset correction learning** in the same Settings
section clears automatic lessons without deleting dictionaries or aliases; individual lessons can
also be removed from the visible list. Quoted material, code, math, citations, links, tables, front
matter, and technical identifiers remain protected in both lanes.

# Citations

Type **@** and start a name — the autocomplete searches your whole
[library](library.qmd) plus the project's own bibliography. Picking one inserts a **citation
chip**: rendered as *(Author, Year)* or as collapsed numerals like *[3,5,9–14]*, your choice —
toggle **Au–Yr** / **[1]** in the References pane (it's stored per document). Numbers assign
themselves in order of appearance and stay correct as you edit.

The bibliography maintains itself. Citing a paper from your library copies its entry into the
project's `references/library.bib` automatically, so the project stays
[self-contained](../concepts/projects-and-files.qmd). Even quicker: **paste a DOI** (or a
doi.org link) straight into the text — Flux fetches the metadata, adds the reference, and
leaves a citation chip where you pasted.

**Double-click a citation chip** to edit its group — add, remove, and reorder the references
cited at that spot as one unit. **Alt+R** opens Reference Search in the margin (mark rows with
**Space**, insert them as one citation with **Enter**); **Alt+C** edits the citation under the
caret.

# Figures

Insert a figure with `/figure` (or **Ctrl+K → Insert figure…**). The picker shows every figure
at full size — scroll (or arrow) through long lists, search by name or caption, and when the
project has more than one canvas, use the dropdown next to the search box to limit the list
(and your search) to a single canvas. In the text, the embed is a
compact **⌗ name chip** with the live figure rendered beneath it — the real thing from
[Figure mode](figure.qmd), with its caption. Captions live on the figure itself (edited in
Figure mode's caption editor), so figure and caption can never drift apart; exports carry them
automatically. Hover the figure for width controls (50% · 75% · 100% · Auto — or drag the
grip), and **Open in Figure** jumps to editing it.

Reference a figure with `@fig-...` — it becomes a live **"Fig 3"** chip whose number stays
correct as figures are added, removed, or reordered (`@tbl-` and `@eq-` work the same way for
tables and equations, with their own autocomplete). Type **@@** for the figure picker, which
can also select specific panels (*Fig 3a,c*). **Double-click** any reference chip to jump to
the thing it points to — a table or equation reference scrolls the editor to its source;
**Ctrl+Enter** follows the reference under the caret.

# Tables

Insert a table with `/table` — it arrives labeled and numbered, with the first header cell
selected so you can just start typing. Everything in the cells renders properly: **bold**,
`code`, math like `$x^2$`, citations, even references to other tables.

While you are reading or writing elsewhere, a table's pipe-text source is out of the way:
it shows as a small blue **▦ Table 3** pill, with the rendered table below it — the same
idea as the pill on a figure's source line. Put the caret in the table and the source comes
straight back, exactly as you typed it. Three ways in, whichever suits:

- **Click a rendered cell** — the caret lands in that cell's source.
- **Click the rendered caption** — the caret lands in the caption text.
- **Click the pill**, or arrow into it from the line above or below.

Move the caret out and it folds away again. Nothing about the `.qmd` on disk changes —
this is only what the editor shows you.

Editing is spreadsheet-shaped:

- **Tab** / **Shift+Tab** move between cells (Tab past the last cell adds a row);
  **Enter** adds a row below — press it on an empty last row to leave the table.
- The pipes align themselves as you type — no manual space-pushing.
- **Ctrl+Alt+R** adds a row, **Ctrl+Alt+C** a column (**+Shift** deletes one);
  **Ctrl+Alt+A** cycles the column's alignment, as does **Alt+click** on a rendered
  header cell.
- Hover the table for **+ Row · + Col · Format · Copy** (Copy puts the table on the
  clipboard tab-separated, ready for Excel or Sheets) — these work whether the source is
  showing or folded away.
- **Paste from Excel/Sheets** and the copied cells become a table — pasted outside one they
  insert a fresh table; pasted inside one they fill cells from the caret. CSV converts via
  **Ctrl+K → Paste as table**.

A table is numbered once it has a caption line — `: Your caption {#tbl-name}` below it —
which `/table` writes for you. A table without one is perfectly fine, it just has no number
to carry, so its pill reads **▦ Table**. Wide tables scroll in the editor and shrink-to-fit
on export so nothing gets cut off. Display math keeps its source line on show: source line,
rendered block below, numbered when labeled.

# The margin

Helper panes summon beside your text and stack in one column:

| Shortcut | Pane |
|---|---|
| **Alt+R** | Reference search — the whole library, filterable (`author:smith year:2020`) |
| **Alt+F** | Figures — zoom/pan any figure, insert it, or open it in Figure mode |
| **Alt+A** | Comments — the review threads on this document |
| **Alt+C** | Citation group — edit the citation at the caret |
| **Alt+T** | Terminal — a real shell (this is where `flux principal` runs nicely) |
| **Alt+J** | Journal Check — the selected journal's rulebook, as advice |

**Alt+P** closes the active pane, and **Escape** always returns focus to your writing.
**Ctrl+Shift+B** hides the margin column entirely; the outline rail's edge
drags to resize. (When idle, the margin shows an ambient background — pick your scene in
Settings › Paper.)

# Two manuscripts side by side

**Alt+click** the Paper icon in the top bar to split the workspace into two Paper panes —
the main text on the left, the supplement (or any other document) on the right. Each pane
has its own outline, margin, and helper panes, and each edits its own document; asking a
pane for a document that's already open in the other pane focuses that pane instead of
opening it twice. There's one terminal between them — summoning it in the other pane moves
it there.

# Comments and review

Select text and click the comment button in the floating toolbar (or press **Ctrl+Alt+M**) to
start a thread anchored to that exact passage. Threads live in the Comments pane: reply,
**Resolve**, reopen, delete. They're stored beside the document — never inside your prose —
and they're the shared review channel with [agents](../agents/collaboration.qmd): an agent
addressing your comments resolves them with a note, and you watch threads close live in your
margin. If the underlying text is edited away, a comment is kept as *Detached* rather than
lost.

**Ctrl+F** is find; **Ctrl+Alt+F** adds replace.

# Export

The **Export** button in the status bar — or **Alt+E** — opens a dialog with two
independent choices: the **file format** (PDF, Word, HTML) and the **journal style**.
Every format saves where you choose, defaulting to the project's `exports/`. Word and
journal-styled PDF run through Quarto (the dialog says so when Quarto isn't installed —
see [Installation](../installation.qmd)); a long render shows its progress and can be
cancelled. Figure renders, captions, and panel references are all resolved during export,
and failures surface as a toast naming what to fix.

## Journal styles

Choosing a journal — **Nature**, say — makes the exported file follow that journal's house
style: how figure and panel references read (`Fig. 1a,b`), how citations are marked
(superscript numerals, before the punctuation), how reference entries are built (all
authors up to five, then `et al.`), what order the sections appear in, and the submission
formatting a manuscript needs (12pt Times, double-spaced, line-numbered).

**Your writing never changes.** The editor keeps Flux's own conventions no matter which
journal is selected — chips, figure references and caption leads look the same whether you
are aiming at Nature or nowhere. Only the exported file and the preview follow the journal,
so switching journals is instant, and switching back loses nothing. Nothing is rewritten in
your manuscript on disk: a journal style is a lens on the way out, not an edit.

Selecting a style is remembered per project, and agents can use the same one from the
terminal with `flux compile --to docx --style nature`.

## Journal Check

**Alt+J** opens **Journal Check**, which reads your manuscript against the selected
journal's rulebook: title and summary-paragraph length, headings the journal doesn't print
(Nature uses neither "Introduction" nor "Results"), missing sections like Data availability,
word budgets, display-item and reference caps, and typed-out figure references that don't
match house style. Click any item to jump to it.

It is **advice, and never blocks an export** — Nature itself says style and length won't
influence consideration at first submission. Switch the panel to *Accepted / final* and the
sections a journal requires at acceptance become warnings rather than notes.

One deliberate limit: Flux formats references it owns — the ones you insert as figure
references — and only *points at* figure references you typed by hand. It cannot tell your
"Figure 2, panel D" from a mention of someone else's Figure 2D, so it never rewrites your
prose.

# Vim, and how the caret feels

For keyboard fans, **Ctrl+K → Enable Vim mode** turns on modal editing, with two flavors:
plain **Vim**, or **flux-ViM** — Vim plus Flux's opt-in refinements (the first: `jj` in insert
mode is Escape). If none of this means anything to you, ignore it happily.

Separately, Settings › Paper offers **Caret motion**: *chase* (the default — the caret
pursues your typing with a lively, immediate feel) or *smooth* (a fixed soft glide).

# Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause → fix |
|---|---|
| A citation chip shows your typed text, dimmed | The key isn't in the project bib or library → check the spelling, or add the paper to the [Library](library.qmd) first |
| Word export is disabled | Quarto isn't installed → [install it](../installation.qmd), restart Flux |
| A journal-styled PDF fails but Word works | Missing LaTeX pieces → the error names the package; see [Installation](../installation.qmd) |
| Journal Check flags a figure reference that is fine | It's advice, not a rule — dismiss it. References to another paper's figures are skipped automatically when an author name is next to them |
| A figure embed shows no caption | The figure has no caption yet → write it in Figure mode (**Alt+C** there) |
| A comment shows as *Detached* | Its anchored text was edited away — the thread is preserved; re-select and start a fresh one if needed |
